primary_meaning: The Garden of Eden as paradise: the original place of perfect creation, innocence, abundance, and unhindered communion with God, later associated with the Fall and eschatological restoration
primary_basis: Genesis 2:8–15 (planting of Eden, trees of life and knowledge, rivers, Adam's placement)
Genesis 3 (temptation, Fall, expulsion from the garden)
Revelation 2:7 and 22:1–5 (tree of life and paradise of God restored in the new creation)

alternatives.meaning: The Church (or the soul of the believer) as an enclosed, cultivated garden of divine love and fruitfulness
basis: Song of Songs 4:12–16; 5:1; 6:2 (enclosed garden, fountain, spices)
Patristic and medieval allegories equating the bride/garden with the Church or soul

alternatives.meaning: Gethsemane as the place of agony, prayer, submission to the Father's will, and betrayal
basis: Matthew 26:36–46; Mark 14:32–42; Luke 22:39–46; John 18:1 (Jesus' prayer and arrest in the garden)

alternatives.meaning: Spiritual growth or the cultivated life of virtue under God's care
basis: Parables and imagery of planting, pruning, and fruitfulness (e.g., John 15)

alternatives.meaning: General fertility, life, or the created order under divine blessing (without specific Edenic or ecclesial reference)
basis: Genesis 1–2 creation motifs; various poetic uses of gardens/orchards in wisdom and prophetic literature

notes: In mainstream Christian biblical interpretation and teaching the term 'Garden' most immediately and commonly evokes Eden as paradise lost and restored; other readings (ecclesial, Gethsemane, spiritual-cultivation) are well-attested but secondary or context-specific. No major tradition treats the term as lacking symbolic content.
